introduction: On the first day of Riḍván in 1863 Bahá’u’lláh announced three things, and the first was that the sword is abolished in this Revelation. The readings gather his repeated statements of it: holy war is “blotted out from the Book,” victory is to be won by words, deeds and character, and “to be killed … is better for you than to kill.” They also look back honestly. The Báb’s early writings still spoke of jihád, the Bábís took up arms in their own defence, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that Moses and Muḥammad fought for the survival of their communities while denying that any Messenger meant faith to be spread by force. Isaiah’s plowshares, the Gospels’ “put up again thy sword,” Paul, the Qur’án’s “no compulsion” and its first, defensive permission to fight, the Dhammapada, Lao Tzu, Ashoka, Locke and Jefferson all point the same way. The psalm that blesses God for teaching hands to war, the law of the conquest in Deuteronomy, the song at the Red Sea and Machiavelli’s maxim about unarmed prophets are here so that the size of the change can be seen.
questions: “Unsheathe the sword of your tongue.” What does it mean to conquer “the citadels of men’s hearts,” and what kinds of speech would be a misuse of this sword?
Why would the abolition of holy war be called the “first Glad-Tidings”? What had religious war done to religion?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains the wars of Moses and Muḥammad as defence. Read Deuteronomy’s law of conquest and the Qur’án’s “begin not hostilities.” How should a believer today relate to the violence in scripture?

“To be killed … is better for you than to kill.” Socrates and Jesus say something close. Is this a rule for individuals, for a religious community, or for governments too? Where do the Bahá’í writings draw that line?
Machiavelli says unarmed prophets are destroyed. What does the survival and spread of the Bahá’í community under persecution suggest?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá told a questioner that force is not the way “even for the right cause.” Israel sang at the Red Sea. What other power do the readings rely on to end injustice, and how long are they prepared to wait?

outside.why: “Beware lest ye shed the blood of anyone … We have abolished the law to wage holy war.” Isaiah’s hope, carved today outside the United Nations: they shall beat their swords into plowshares; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
“Unsheathe the sword of your tongue.” The Book of Revelation gives its conquering Christ no other weapon: out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword.
Hearts are conquered by utterance. Byron: words are things, and a small drop of ink, falling like dew upon a thought, produces that which makes thousands, perhaps millions, think.
“The triumph of a single pure deed is … greater than the victory of an army.” Proverbs: he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city.
The Dhammapada: if one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
The first glad-tidings is that “the law of holy war hath been blotted out.” Jesus at his arrest: all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
“Shed not blood.” The Qur’án: whosoever killeth a human being, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind.
“We have annulled the rule of the sword … and substituted for it the power born of the utterance of men.” Paul: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.
Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
A believer asks for the means to fight for his Lord, and is refused. Jesus to Pilate: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight.
“Weapons have been transformed into means of peace.” Micah: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid.
God has ordained in place of the sword “loving-kindness.” Proverbs: a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
Some still interpret “victory” by their own delusions. Two disciples wished to call down fire on a village, and Jesus rebuked them: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.

Assistance “has never been and is not by the sword.” The Letter to the Ephesians arms its readers entirely with virtues: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Holy war is forbidden and “fellowship with the followers of all religions” enjoined. The Qur’án’s own rule for presenting faith: call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way.
The principle that faith cannot be forced was already in the Book of those who waged holy war. The Qur’án: there is no compulsion in religion.
The first word spoken in the garden of Riḍván was that “the sword is abolished.” Lao Tzu: arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen, hateful to all creatures.

“During the time of the Apostle of God … the ordinance of holy war was revealed.” The first verse that permitted fighting gives its reason: sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged.
And its limit: fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.

The Báb at first reaffirmed jihád as “one of the branches of religion.” Scripture before him had sung of it: blessed be the Lord my strength which teacheth my hands to war. What had religious war been for, in the view of those who practised it, and why do the readings say its time is over?

Bahá’u’lláh recalls the bloodshed of earlier dispensations without softening it. The law of Moses for the conquest of Canaan: thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth. How should believers today read such commands in their own scriptures?

The early Muslims “were commanded to defend themselves.” The builders of Jerusalem’s wall worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, having made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch.

Moses fought when attacked; Christ’s three years were of another kind. Even so, on the last night Jesus said: he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one. When two were shown him he said, It is enough.
And when one of them was used: put up again thy sword into his place.

Muḥammad “sanctioned war for the preservation of the lives of His followers.” Machiavelli thought every founder needed arms: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Bahá’u’lláh forbade his followers to fight even in self-defence of the Faith. What is the history of unarmed religions an argument for?

“No Divine Messenger ever … suggested that the sword be used in promulgating his teachings.” John Locke: every man has commission to admonish, exhort, convince another of error; but to compel with the sword belongs to none but the magistrate, and not in matters of belief.

“A faith born of sword thrusts could hardly be relied upon.” Jefferson’s statute for Virginia: no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship; all men shall be free to profess, and by argument to maintain, their opinions in matters of religion.
The law of jihád was “a veritable firebrand.” Pascal: men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.

“There can be no war where there is religion. All we have is a hollow sham.” Mark Twain wrote out what a congregation’s prayer for victory really asks: help us to tear their soldiers to bloody shreds with our shells.
Wilfred Owen, from the trenches of a war blessed in every church: the old Lie: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori.

“Fighting, and the employment of force, even for the right cause,” is not the way. Israel’s first song after the Red Sea praises force used for the oppressed: the Lord is a man of war. Liberation movements have sung it ever since. What does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá expect to accomplish what force cannot?
The Dhammapada on why force does not settle things: victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy.
“To be killed in the path of His good pleasure is better for you than to kill.” Socrates: if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do injustice.
Jesus: I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
In the beginning they defended themselves; later “they had no fear” and did not. Tertullian of the early Christians: the oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow.
Some believers fought despite the prohibition, “but God hath pardoned whom He willeth.” Jesus: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
With physical warfare forbidden, “the doors of spiritual conquests are opened.” Paul: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.

“There is no need for sword or spear.” The emperor Ashoka, after his conquest of Kalinga and its hundred thousand dead, had his remorse cut in rock: even those who do wrong should be forgiven where forgiveness is possible.

“That sword killed, this one gives life; that one destroyed, this one builds.” The Qur’án on the weapon that ends an enmity: repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity, will become as though he was a bosom friend.

deuteronomy-save-alive-nothing-that-brea.text: But of the cities of these people, which the Lord thy God doth give thee for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth: But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee
